name: PolyRoute Delivery Driver Weathershell
description:
PolyRoute is one of GLMZ's dominant last-mile delivery networks, and the Weathershell is what their drivers wear through the city's full meteorological range — acid-tinged lake squalls, the deep cold of Great Lakes winters, and the wet heat that settles over the megacity's lower districts in summer. The jacket is a three-layer construction: an outer shell of hydrophobic ripstop that sheds water and resists the mild chemical content of GLMZ's precipitation, a thermal-regulating mid-layer that adjusts insulation based on exertion level, and a moisture-wicking inner face. The exterior is a medium grey with PolyRoute's route-arrow logo in orange at the chest and back, and high-visibility retroreflective striping along the sleeves.

A GPS-conductive thread network runs through the jacket's left sleeve, connecting to a wrist-worn routing display that pulls live delivery manifests, traffic data, and route optimization from PolyRoute's logistics AI. The jacket includes a chest-mounted scanner holster for package verification hardware. BCI-compatible collar port allows hands-free navigation for drivers with neural interface setups. The Weathershell is geneware-tolerant at the back and waist — tail accommodation gussets are standard, and the hood has adjustable side clearance for ear configurations. PolyRoute drivers are contractors, not employees, which means the jacket is technically a rental deducted from earnings — a financial arrangement that generates significant resentment among the workforce.
cultural_context: The grey-and-orange of PolyRoute is everywhere in GLMZ, a constant reminder of the gig economy that underpins the city's consumption. Drivers develop intense familiarity with every district's rhythms, and the Weathershell marks them as people who know the city's back routes, service corridors, and unofficial shortcuts better than anyone. That knowledge has value far beyond package delivery.
story_hooks: A PolyRoute driver discovers their GPS thread network has been logging not just their routes but detailed interior scans of every building they've entered for delivery — data PolyRoute has been selling to an undisclosed third party.
A series of Weathershell jackets are recovered from a Tier 1 warehouse, all with their GPS threads manually extracted — someone is building a fleet of untraceable delivery drivers.
A driver's routing AI begins sending them to addresses that don't exist in any official registry, and the packages they're delivering have no sender information.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian three-layer jacket with a distinctly functional silhouette. Medium grey base with high-contrast orange route-arrow branding at chest and back. High-visibility retroreflective striping runs vertically along sleeves in bright white. The overall impression is industrial-practical—designed to be seen moving through urban sprawl at speed.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed through the torso with reinforced shoulder articulation for repetitive reaching and scanning motions. Geneware-tolerant—tail accommodation gussets at lower back and waist, adjustable hood side clearance for non-standard ear augmentations. Sleeves cut long enough to accommodate wrist-worn routing displays without binding.
physical_description.primary_material: Three-layer composite: hydrophobic ripstop outer shell (chemical-resistant treatment for acid-tinged precipitation), thermally-regulating mid-layer (exertion-responsive insulation), moisture-wicking inner face. GPS-conductive thread network woven through left sleeve structure.
physical_description.texture: Outer shell has subtle ripstop texture with slight technical sheen. Retroreflective striping has micro-prismatic texture visible at angles. Inner lining is soft, quick-dry synthetic. BCI-compatible collar port sits as a smooth recessed interface point.
physical_description.color_scheme: Medium grey base (corporate neutrality, dust-resistant). PolyRoute orange (#FF6B35 approximate) on chest and back logos. High-visibility white retroreflective striping on sleeves. Subtle grey-on-grey tonal variation in thermal layer visible at sleeve cuffs and hood interior.
physical_description.closures: Primary center zip with friction-fit storm flap overlay. Magnetic snaps at cuff closure for quick one-handed fastening while holding packages. Hood cinch uses friction-lock toggles. Chest scanner holster secured with reinforced hook-and-loop.
distinctive_features: GPS-conductive thread network in left sleeve connecting to routing display interface
Chest-mounted scanner holster with reinforced retention stitching
BCI-compatible recessed collar port (upper left, minimalist design)
Geneware accommodation gussets at lower back and waist (tail-capable)
Adjustable hood side clearance for non-standard ear/head augmentations
Retroreflective striping runs full sleeve length for visibility in low-light districts
Route-arrow logo (PolyRoute branding) occupies 40% of chest—marks wearer as contractor
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 1-2 contractor uniform (issued, not owned—rental-deducted from earnings, which signals precarity despite tier classification)
physical_description.cultural_context: PolyRoute delivery driver. Wearer is a gig-economy contractor navigating GLMZ's districts as logistics node. The jacket marks them as someone who knows the city's back routes, service corridors, and unofficial shortcuts better than corporate planners. Knowledge-bearer and visible urban worker simultaneously. Generates ambivalent respect and resentment—essential infrastructure worker treated as disposable labor.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in. Visible creasing at sleeve articulation points from repetitive scanning motions. Light weathering on shoulders and hood from acid-rain exposure (faint etching patterns). Holster shows wear polish from package scanner contact. Zipper slider may show minor patina. Despite heavy use, the ripstop resists tears—these jackets survive the job.
